title: Atlantic City Mob Land Deals and Racketeering Enterprise Participation
description_short: Atlantic City Mob Land Deals and Racketeering Enterprise Participation
description_medium: Reports describe Trump’s dealings with contractors and developers linked to organized crime during Atlantic City casino construction. CNN reported that S&A Concrete, controlled by Anthony Salerno and Paul Castellano, supplied concrete for Trump Plaza condominiums; Politico also recounts FBI questions about Trump’s dealings with Teamsters official John Cody. These reports identify mob-linked business contacts, but do not establish that Trump joined a racketeering enterprise or committed a crime.
description_long: Donald Trump purchased casino land in Atlantic City from Philadelphia mobster Salvatore Testa at double market value while using $8 million in overpriced concrete from companies controlled by Genovese and Gambino crime family heads 'Fat Tony' Salerno and Paul Castellano, with federal investigation concluding Trump Plaza 'most likely benefited from connections to racketeering' through systematic organized crime collaboration. The comprehensive mob collaboration included paying $1.1 million for property that mobsters had purchased for $195,000 in 1977, demonstrating willingness to pay inflated prices to organized crime figures while using construction companies controlled by mafia families that provided union peace through criminal intimidation. The racketeering participation extended to Trump's decade-long relationship with Scarfo family banker while construction involved companies linked to Philadelphia mobsters Nicademo 'Little Nicky' Scarfo and nephew Phillip 'Crazy Phil' Leonetti, creating systematic criminal enterprise that enabled casino construction through organized crime networks. Trump's organized crime collaboration violated federal racketeering laws by participating in criminal enterprise that used violence and intimidation to control construction industry while generating profits through systematic overcharging and union manipulation that constituted organized criminal activity. The mob land deals created federal investigation that documented Trump's willing participation in racketeering enterprise, with prosecutors concluding his casino construction benefited from organized crime connections that provided inflated contracts and union peace through criminal coercion rather than legitimate business practices. The Atlantic City racketeering established Trump's systematic approach to organized crime relationships, demonstrating willingness to participate in criminal enterprises while using mafia connections to circumvent legitimate business competition through systematic collaboration with violent criminal organizations that controlled construction industry through intimidation and murder.
subcategory: Organized Crime Collaboration and Racketeering Enterprise
notes: Reason: The populated long description alleges criminal participation, illegal racketeering and specific land and contract figures that the supplied reporting does not establish.

Proposed correction: Replace the existing long text with a source-attributed account of reported business dealings with mob-linked suppliers and developers; remove unsupported criminal findings and transaction figures.

title: Trump: Under pressure from Trump, FDA lies about coronavirus treatment
description_short: Trump: Under pressure from Trump, FDA lies about coronavirus treatment
description_medium: At a White House briefing on August 23, 2020, FDA Commissioner Stephen Hahn announced an emergency-use authorization for convalescent plasma as a COVID-19 treatment. He described data as showing a “35% improvement in survival,” and Trump presented the authorization as an achievement. Hahn apologized the next day, saying he had overstated the benefits and should have described a relative risk reduction. The sequence does not establish that Trump pressured Hahn to lie.
description_long: The FDA authorized emergency use of convalescent plasma for COVID-19 on August 23, 2020. At a White House briefing, Commissioner Stephen Hahn described the evidence as showing a “35% improvement in survival,” while Trump praised the authorization as a major achievement. The announcement followed Trump’s public criticism of the FDA the previous day, when he accused the agency of delaying treatments. The timing raised concerns about political pressure, but it does not by itself show that Hahn’s statement was made at Trump’s direction or that he knowingly lied. The next day Hahn said criticism of his remarks was justified and clarified that the data showed a relative risk reduction, not an absolute reduction. Convalescent plasma uses antibodies in blood donated by people who have recovered from infection; the emergency authorization was a regulatory decision, not a new treatment discovery. This episode records an imprecise public description of preliminary evidence, the commissioner’s correction and a highly publicized authorization. It does not establish the causal claim in the title that Trump pressured the FDA to lie.
notes: Reason: Hahn corrected his efficacy statement, but the available account does not establish that Trump pressured him or that the original statement was knowingly false.
Proposed correction: Describe the emergency authorization, Hahn’s overstated claim and next-day clarification; attribute the pressure allegation unless evidence establishes causation.

title: Donald Trump stops COVID relief in Congress until after the election, if he wins
description_short: Donald Trump stops COVID relief in Congress until after the election, if he wins
description_medium: On October 6, 2020, Donald Trump ordered his representatives to stop negotiating another COVID-19 relief package until after the election, saying talks could resume immediately after he won. The decision came as Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin and House Speaker Nancy Pelosi had been negotiating and the Federal Reserve chair warned that more fiscal support was needed. Trump also told Senate Republicans to focus on confirming Amy Coney Barrett. The announcement halted the administration’s negotiations during the campaign.
description_long: On October 6, 2020, Donald Trump announced that he had instructed his representatives to stop negotiating a further COVID-19 relief package until after the election, adding that a bill would pass “immediately after I win.” The announcement came after he spoke with congressional Republican leaders, while Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin and House Speaker Nancy Pelosi had been negotiating. The White House had recently offered a $400 weekly jobless benefit and discussed a $1.6 trillion relief package, which Pelosi rejected; many Senate Republicans opposed a bill above $1 trillion. Trump also asked Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell to focus on confirming Supreme Court nominee Amy Coney Barrett. Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell had warned that more fiscal support was needed to keep the fragile recovery from weakening. Trump’s post publicly tied the timing of federal relief talks to the election outcome. The record establishes his announcement and its immediate negotiating context; it does not by itself establish the eventual effect on aid recipients or the later legislative outcome.

title: Trump: Giuliani, Trump begin calls to Arizona GOP to push election fraud claims
description_short: Trump: Giuliani, Trump begin calls to Arizona GOP to push election fraud claims
description_medium: In mid-November 2020, Rudy Giuliani called Arizona Senate President Karen Fann seeking help advancing election-fraud claims in the state, according to the timeline. Donald Trump also called Fann to thank her for her efforts. The account places the calls broadly in mid-November but does not establish their exact dates. On December 2, Fann told a constituent by email that she had spoken with Giuliani.
description_long: In mid-November 2020, Rudy Giuliani contacted Arizona Senate President Karen Fann and asked her to help promote claims of election fraud in the state. Donald Trump also called Fann to thank her for her efforts. Fann later referred to a conversation with Giuliani in a December 2 email to a constituent. The timeline does not identify the precise dates of Trump’s or Giuliani’s calls, give a transcript of either conversation, or specify exactly what help Giuliani requested. It also does not say that Fann agreed to act or that the calls changed Arizona’s election procedures or results. The available account documents direct outreach to a state legislative leader while the Trump campaign was challenging the 2020 election outcome. The calls’ timing and stated purpose matter, but the event date should remain approximate: the source places them in mid-November, while December 2 is the date of Fann’s later email. The calls should not be assigned a specific day without a record establishing it.
notes: Reason: The supplied synopsis says the calls occurred sometime in mid-November and explicitly says their exact date is unknown, which conflicts with the record’s single-day date.
Proposed correction: Use a mid-November date range or document the exact call date before retaining a precise event date.

title: Trump: Rosen stops Trump from using the DOJ to steal the election
description_short: Trump: Rosen stops Trump from using the DOJ to steal the election
description_medium: After William Barr resigned, Donald Trump pressed acting Attorney General Jeffrey Rosen to use the Justice Department to support election lawsuits and investigate alleged voter fraud. Trump then sought to replace Rosen with Jeffrey Clark, who supported Trump’s fraud claims. Rosen, Deputy Attorney General Richard Donoghue and other senior officials prepared to resign if Clark took over. Trump ultimately kept Rosen after a meeting with department and White House officials.
description_long: After Attorney General William Barr resigned in December 2020, Donald Trump pressed acting Attorney General Jeffrey Rosen to have the Justice Department support the campaign’s election lawsuits and investigate claims of voter fraud. Rosen refused, citing the department’s findings that there was no significant fraud. Trump then sought to replace Rosen with Jeffrey Clark, a Justice Department official who had told Trump he believed fraud affected the result. When Rosen learned of the plan, he and Deputy Attorney General Richard Donoghue contacted other senior officials; they agreed they would resign if Clark took over. On January 3, Rosen and Donoghue met with Trump, Clark and White House lawyers. Rosen, Donoghue and White House Counsel Pat Cipollone urged Trump not to proceed, while Justice Department legal chief Steven Engel said he would resign and others would follow. After nearly three hours, Trump decided not to fire Rosen. The episode shows an effort to use departmental leadership to advance election claims and the officials’ response. The title’s “steal the election” wording is a characterization, not a quoted legal finding.
notes: Reason: The account establishes pressure to use DOJ for lawsuits and fraud investigations and a proposed replacement of Rosen, but “steal the election” is not a quoted finding and overstates what the source directly establishes.
Proposed correction: Retitle to describe Trump’s effort to replace Rosen with Clark and the senior officials’ resistance.
